## Where this applies

- Inference: Define return-to-performance "success" for Baylor athletes with several criteria, as Fleisig does (staying healthy, then stats matched to age or context, not one game back) [54:02]. The decision is how Applied Performance reports RTP outcomes to Athletic Medicine and coaches.
- Inference: Compare a returning athlete to an age- and role-expected trajectory, not to their pre-injury numbers, because the talk argues post-surgery performance drifts with age [21:39]. This applies to VALD force plate and GPS return benchmarks.
- Inference: If Applied Performance supports baseball, track season and year-round throwing exposure (pitches, innings, months) and fatigue flags per pitcher, because exposure and pitching when fatigued were the strongest risk markers in his data [31:58], [33:31].
- Inference: Build a reference range for a force plate or GPS metric from healthy, high-performing Baylor athletes at a position (mean and standard deviation), as Fleisig did for mechanics [55:33], and use it as a flag, not a verdict.
- Inference: Use the "fatigue is individual; next day matters" rule to shape football practice monitoring: pair daily objective data with trainer and coach knowledge of the athlete [50:29], [51:30].

## Eric's baseline

- Eric's baseline: mRSI from daily CMJ replaced subjective wellness surveys as the readiness marker because it is objective, consistent and actionable; surveys were dropped after athletes gamed them, but kept for return-to-play (Eric's SportSmith article). The talk partly conflicts: Fleisig relies on trainer and athlete next-day report and says fatigue cannot be measured in the moment [50:29]. The baseline keeps subjective input in RTP, which fits his context.
- Eric's baseline: a trained coach's eye matters as much as technology for daily assessment (course material, speaker unconfirmed). The talk agrees, with trainers as the key reader of fatigue [51:30].
- Eric's baseline: injury risk is reduced, not eliminated; smooth, gradual progression of load (course material, speaker unconfirmed). The talk extends this with overuse and exposure evidence from youth baseball.
- Eric's baseline: Applied Performance supports RTP decisions with information; no RTP criteria are documented in the corpus. The talk offers a multi-part success definition that could fill a gap [54:02].
- Eric's baseline: force plate metrics are chosen by the output, driver, strategy and symmetry framework (Hawkin Dynamics). The talk's reference-range method extends it but does not replace it.
- Eric's baseline: no formal injury-risk model is attributed to Eric. No direct link to Fleisig's risk odds beyond this.

## What would have to be true

- Return definition: agreement with Athletic Medicine and coaches on criteria and time windows before any return is judged.
- Age-expected comparison: a comparison group of similar athletes, with enough players per position to estimate a trend.
- Exposure tracking: reliable counts (pitches, innings, months of throwing) from baseball staff; without them the odds cannot be checked.
- Reference ranges: enough healthy athletes at a position, same test protocol every time, and a check that the range predicts something at Baylor.
- Fatigue process: trainers and coaches who see the athlete daily and a written trigger for what happens when they flag him.

## Do not apply when

- The data are pitchers (baseball overhead throwing); do not transfer elbow torque, UCL return rates or pitch-count figures to football or other sports.
- The youth findings (500 pitchers, over 100 innings) are not college-level thresholds; do not set a college innings limit from them.
- The 4 to 1, 5 to 1 and 36 to 1 odds are retrospective and recall-based; do not treat them as causal or as predictive risk scores for an individual.
- Reference ranges defined by high velocity and health are partly circular, and the talk reports poor mechanics predicted injury about half the time [58:38]; do not use an out-of-range value to restrict an athlete by itself.
- Sample sizes are small and partly unpublished (38 pitchers in one study, the spring training work); do not generalize a result from one or two studies.
- Vendor devices shown (motion tools from a company the speaker advises) were not validated in the talk [41:13].

## First step

List the last two seasons' return-to-performance cases and write, for each, the four pieces from the talk (did they return, did they stay healthy, stats versus age-matched expectation, time to return) in a simple sheet. Do not share it until you have checked it against Athletic Medicine records.

---
type: video-summary
video_id: wWV7s5CSSpY
title: "2012 SSAC: Football Analytics"
event: SSAC12 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
speakers: [Mike Hancock (student lead), Eric Mangini, Matt Roth, Bill Barnwell, "Prague" of the San Francisco 49ers (caption spelling), Andrea Kramer (moderator)]
topics: [american-football, front-office, decision-making, competitive-advantage, injury-health]
confidence: untested
caption_source: auto
status: draft
---

## Summary

A moderated panel with a former head coach, an active player, a writer and a front-office executive on where analytics fits in the NFL. The panel says use is uneven: few teams invest the time and money, and buy-in needs the GM, head coach and continuity [03:10]. They name three areas: game management and self-scouting, personnel evaluation, and salary cap work [03:41]. Recurring themes are boiling data down so players can use it, judging decisions by process and not outcome, what stats miss (role players, intangibles), and the draft as the biggest open opportunity. The talk is experience and opinion, with no datasets shown, so it fits "untested".

## Key claims

- Analytics is not universally accepted in football, and few teams spend the time, money and effort to promote it [02:38].
- Analytics needs GM and head coach involvement and organizational commitment, and staff turnover undermines it [03:10].
- Results take a long time to show [03:41].
- The panel names three uses: game management and self-scouting, personnel evaluation, and salary cap management [03:41].
- Teams have plenty of data; the analytic process is making sense of it and deciding what is relevant [05:15].
- A tendency report of about 50 items was cut to a "top ten" list of what players should take into the game, installed midweek as part of the scouting report [06:45].
- A player used the percentages to decide when to take a calculated risk, and worked film to raise the percentage on the remaining share [09:21].
- A designated person outside the coaching staff, upstairs, can relay what the numbers say during the game, because sideline decisions are fast and pressured [10:53].
- In-game uses named: timeouts, fourth down, extra point versus two-point try [12:25].
- Coaches need a good-process and bad-process, good-outcome and bad-outcome frame, because a good outcome can come from bad process [13:56].
- Analytics moves odds a little (the speaker's example is 49 to 55 percent), and several good-process, good-outcome results in a row may be needed before people buy in [14:28], [15:01].
- Coaches can look risk-averse because criticism follows a failed aggressive choice; icing the kicker is the example, which the speaker says studies show has no effect [15:32], [16:03].

## Where this applies

- Inference: Cut a recurring coach-facing report (weekly GPS or force plate summary) to a fixed short list of items per group, the way the panel cut about 50 opponent tendencies to a top ten so players could act on it [06:45]. The decision is which few metrics go on the page each week.
- Inference: Treat recruiting grades the way the panel treats scout grades: define vague terms before they are used, and audit each grader's accuracy by position after outcomes are known [35:01], [44:18]. This applies to how PFF-based and staff grades are combined in recruiting grading.
- Inference: For speed evaluation, check whether the flying segment (for example the 30 to 40 yard split or max velocity on GPS) separates athletes better than total 40 time, as the panel claims for receivers [36:34]. The decision is which speed metric goes in a position profile.
- Inference: Run a short process-versus-outcome review of return-to-performance and load decisions (was the call sound given what was known, separately from how it turned out) to avoid judging decisions only by results [13:56].
- Inference: Compare tracked practice exposure (plays or GPS load) against a planned cap per athlete, as the panel did with a play cap [45:50]; Baylor has GPS data to do this more finely.

## Eric's baseline

- Eric's baseline: a small number of valid, reliable tests mapped to clear KPI categories beats an exhaustive battery, and data collection is judged on cost versus insight (method-baseline, Testing and Philosophy sections). The talk agrees with cutting to the few items that matter.
- Eric's baseline: 0 to 10 m is read as an acceleration score and 30 to 40 m as a speed score, with 40 m peak velocity derived from the 30 to 40 split (AP Assessment Manual V12, author uncertain, possibly legacy). The talk's flying-20 claim is consistent with reading the later split separately; it extends, it does not conflict.
- Eric's baseline: injury risk is reduced, not eliminated, and progressions are smooth and gradual (course material, speaker unconfirmed). The talk's "moving the needle, not certainty" framing agrees [14:28].
- Eric's baseline: early GPS and load monitoring bred a culture of fear that pushed teams toward under-training (course material, speaker unconfirmed). The talk's play caps [45:50] sit in tension with this: a cap can protect or can under-prepare, so the talk is not evidence that lower exposure is better.
- Eric's baseline: Applied Performance supports Athletics Performance and Athletic Medicine decisions rather than making them. The talk's designated upstairs analyst [10:53] is a similar supporting role.

## What would have to be true

- Report trimming: coaches must agree which decisions the report serves, and you need a few weeks of the current report to see which items were used.
- Grader audit: enough graded recruits with known later outcomes at each position to see anything; a handful per position will not show grader skill.
- Flying-split check: a same-athlete sample with both total and split times (and GPS max velocity) and some performance outcome to compare to; the panel showed no data for its claim.
- Process review: a written record of what was known at decision time, kept before the outcome.
- Exposure cap: a defined cap per position and session type, agreed with Athletic Medicine and coaches.

## Do not apply when

- The point is about NFL contracts, dead money, draft value charts or the rookie scale [24:48], [29:21]. College has none of these mechanisms in the same form, so do not port the cap arguments.
- The panel's 2012 NFL view of GPS (it did not work with pads and contact) is one team's experience from then; do not use it to rule GPS out today [45:50].
- A receiver flying-20 claim rests on the panelist's assertion and NFL combine data; do not apply it to college positions, non-receivers or one team's small sample.
- A play cap would under-prepare athletes if set without regard to role and session type (see baseline above).
- Intangible grades can be confounded by outcome: the speaker warns that memorable successes (for example Tebow) hide forgotten failures [43:15].

## First step

Take one existing weekly report and draft a version with only the top three metrics per position group; show it to one coach next to the current one and record which they use. Keep the original.

## Summary

Glenn Fleisig of the American Sports Medicine Institute explains the rise of ulnar collateral ligament (Tommy John) surgery in baseball and what his group's data say about it. He covers the stress on the elbow, how often pitchers return after surgery, risk factors, and prevention. His headline finding: too much pitching, and especially pitching while fatigued, is the strongest risk factor he has found [33:31]. Curveballs were not shown to be more dangerous than fastballs, though he says they were not proven safe [52:31]. He closes with MLB and youth prevention efforts (PitchSmart) and wearable and camera biomechanics tools, some from a company he advises [41:13].

## Key claims

- Professional UCL surgeries were steady for about 20 years, then climbed, so the rise is not a one-year fluke [07:42].
- About 16 percent of professional pitchers have had the surgery, with a higher share among major leaguers that he attributes to more years pitching [08:13], [09:14].
- The ligament has to resist most of the elbow stress in the cocked position, and cadaver work showed the ligament alone cannot take that load, so muscle and other tissue share it [16:28], [17:00].
- The surgery does not improve velocity or performance; he believes the two studies that found performance down toward age-expected levels [21:39], [22:10].
- Return to the majors takes about a year and a half in published studies, about 12 months in his group's data [22:40], [24:15].
- In a spring training comparison, pitchers who had returned from surgery matched never-injured pitchers on flexibility and mechanics [28:21], [28:52].
- Youth pitchers with over 100 competitive innings in a year had over three times the risk of serious elbow or shoulder injury [31:58].
- Retrospective comparisons linked surgery to pitching often when fatigued, pitching many months a year, and high pitch counts in a game [32:30], [33:00].
- Activity in children is polarized: a few do too much, many too little; moderate activity is the goal [36:38], [38:10].
- Lab and field studies did not show curveballs to be more dangerous than fastballs; he advises young pitchers to learn fastball and changeup first [39:41], [40:12], [52:31].
- Fatigue is individual; it cannot be measured in the moment, so coaches and trainers who know the athlete, plus next-day symptoms, are the guide [50:29], [51:30].
- Poor mechanics are shown to increase arm stress, but it is not proven that higher stress causes more injury [58:38].
- Drug-driven muscle gains can outpace ligaments and tendons (his statement, no data shown) [48:54].
- The ultimate goal is tracking pitchers' biomechanics in games, which is not yet available [42:13].

## Numbers and definitions

- Elbow torque in the cocked position: about 100 newton-meters, compared to holding five 12 lb bowling balls on a string [15:27], [15:58]. The clip captions read "512b", which is garbled; 5 x 12 = 60 lb matches [10:45].
- The ligament withstands about 55 percent of the stress, which he gives as 55 newton-meters [16:28].
- Elbow speed 2,300 degrees per second (caption "2,300 de per second") [14:22].
- Elbow about 90 degrees bent at foot contact [14:22].
- Surgeries by age and level: 16 percent of professional pitchers have had it; about 15 percent of minor leaguers and 25 percent of major leaguers [08:13], [08:44]. The 16 percent and 25 percent come from a study he says is not yet published.
- Return rates: about 80 percent return; about 67 percent return and stay [22:10]. His group's rate is about 80 percent, regardless of high school, college or pro [23:11], [56:34].
- Return time: about 18 months in the studies vs about 12 months in his group's data [22:40], [24:15].
- Three published studies: one covering 1974 to 2012, one of 147 pitchers since 1999, one of 38 recent pitchers with PitchFX data since 2008 (caption names "Ericson", "mcne/mockney", "Jang"; spellings unverified) [20:04], [20:35], [21:05].
- Spring training study: 40 post-surgery vs 40 never-injured pitchers, both about 85 mph [25:47], [28:21].
- Youth cohort: about 500 pitchers followed weekly during a season and yearly for 10 years; over 100 innings in any year meant more than three times the risk [31:28], [31:58].
- Odds from retrospective questions: pitching over 80 pitches in a game, 4 to 1; more than 8 months a year, 5 to 1; pitching often when fatigued, 36 to 1 [32:30], [33:00], [33:31]. The "8 months" figure and "$36 to $1" wording are caption-dependent.
- Lab: over 2,000 pitchers tested; 12 cameras, about 40 markers, 500 frames per second (captions say "pictures") [13:20], [43:13].
- Proper mechanics definition: about 150 pitchers tested with healthy arms for at least a year and high fastball velocity; mean and standard deviation of each measure [55:03], [55:33].
- Fastball velocity averaged about 2 mph higher since 2002 and the count of pitchers averaging 94 mph doubled (from a clip in the talk, not Fleisig's own data) [10:15].
- Success after surgery in the studies: at least 10 major league games [53:32], [54:02].
- Latin American pitchers: same rate, about 16 percent [57:05], [57:36].

## Methods and frameworks named

- 3D motion capture lab with reflective markers; kinematics measured, kinetics (forces and torque) calculated from motion [11:46], [12:17].
- Cadaver testing of ligament strength [16:28].
- Case comparison of pitchers with and without surgery on history questions [32:30].
- Prospective youth cohort with weekly and yearly follow-up [31:28].
- Spring training field labs with MLB, four mechanical hypotheses (compensation, holding back, "inverted W", low elbow then raise) [25:47], [26:47], [27:18].
- Reference-range definition of proper mechanics from healthy high-velocity pitchers [55:03].
- MLB elbow task force and the PitchSmart guidelines and risk survey [45:49], [46:19], [46:50].

## Limits and open questions

- Some figures come from unpublished work (16 percent, 25 percent, spring training study at the time) [08:13], [28:21].
- Spring training study: minor leaguers only, measured only after return, and only successes [28:52], [29:22], [29:53]. No pre-injury mechanics.
- Retrospective odds (4 to 1, 5 to 1, 36 to 1) rely on recall, not controlled prospective measures, and he says himself he did not say causation beyond this [32:30], [33:31].
- Proper mechanics is defined by fast velocity and health, so the benchmark is partly circular; in follow-up, poor mechanics predicted injury about half the time, and the link from arm stress to injury is unproven [55:03], [58:38].
- Curveball result: failure to prove danger is not proof of safety, as he says [52:31].
- Long-term outcomes for surgery at young ages are unknown [56:34].
- Institutional and commercial interest: he advises MLB, Little League, USA Baseball and modus, and is helping develop its devices [06:08], [41:13].
- The chair says the talk is on a panel; the clip from another professor on ball pressure is unrelated to the talk [01:31].
- Caption garbles: "thousand pictures" (likely pitchers) [23:11]; "mcne", "mockney", "Ericson", "Jang", "Kane c a i n" unverified; "sa young" is Cy Young, caption spelling [13:51].

## Q&A

- How do you know when a pitcher is fatigued: individual, not measurable in the moment, rely on knowing the pitcher, trainers and next-day symptoms [49:59], [50:29], [51:30].
- Split-finger fastball stress: not studied; fastballs, curveballs and sliders are stressful and changeups less so [52:01], [53:02].
- What counts as return success: the studies used at least 10 major league games; he prefers staying healthy and stats matching age [53:32], [54:02].
- How proper mechanics were determined: healthy, fast pitchers' mean and standard deviation [54:32], [55:33].
- Age at surgery: about 80 percent return across levels; long-term outcomes for the young are unknown [56:03], [56:34].
- Latin American pitchers: same rate as Americans [57:05].
- Did poor-mechanics pitchers get injured: about half did, half did not; arm stress-to-injury link not proven [58:06], [58:38].

## Where this applies

- Inference: Define return-to-performance "success" for Baylor athletes with several criteria, as Fleisig does (staying healthy, then stats matched to age or context, not one game back) [54:02]. The decision is how Applied Performance reports RTP outcomes to Athletic Medicine and coaches.
- Inference: Compare a returning athlete to an age- and role-expected trajectory, not to their pre-injury numbers, because the talk argues post-surgery performance drifts with age [21:39]. This applies to VALD force plate and GPS return benchmarks.
- Inference: If Applied Performance supports baseball, track season and year-round throwing exposure (pitches, innings, months) and fatigue flags per pitcher, because exposure and pitching when fatigued were the strongest risk markers in his data [31:58], [33:31].
- Inference: Build a reference range for a force plate or GPS metric from healthy, high-performing Baylor athletes at a position (mean and standard deviation), as Fleisig did for mechanics [55:33], and use it as a flag, not a verdict.
- Inference: Use the "fatigue is individual; next day matters" rule to shape football practice monitoring: pair daily objective data with trainer and coach knowledge of the athlete [50:29], [51:30].

## Eric's baseline

- Eric's baseline: mRSI from daily CMJ replaced subjective wellness surveys as the readiness marker because it is objective, consistent and actionable; surveys were dropped after athletes gamed them, but kept for return-to-play (Eric's SportSmith article). The talk partly conflicts: Fleisig relies on trainer and athlete next-day report and says fatigue cannot be measured in the moment [50:29]. The baseline keeps subjective input in RTP, which fits his context.
- Eric's baseline: a trained coach's eye matters as much as technology for daily assessment (course material, speaker unconfirmed). The talk agrees, with trainers as the key reader of fatigue [51:30].
- Eric's baseline: injury risk is reduced, not eliminated; smooth, gradual progression of load (course material, speaker unconfirmed). The talk extends this with overuse and exposure evidence from youth baseball.
- Eric's baseline: Applied Performance supports RTP decisions with information; no RTP criteria are documented in the corpus. The talk offers a multi-part success definition that could fill a gap [54:02].
- Eric's baseline: force plate metrics are chosen by the output, driver, strategy and symmetry framework (Hawkin Dynamics). The talk's reference-range method extends it but does not replace it.
- Eric's baseline: no formal injury-risk model is attributed to Eric. No direct link to Fleisig's risk odds beyond this.

## What would have to be true

- Return definition: agreement with Athletic Medicine and coaches on criteria and time windows before any return is judged.
- Age-expected comparison: a comparison group of similar athletes, with enough players per position to estimate a trend.
- Exposure tracking: reliable counts (pitches, innings, months of throwing) from baseball staff; without them the odds cannot be checked.
- Reference ranges: enough healthy athletes at a position, same test protocol every time, and a check that the range predicts something at Baylor.
- Fatigue process: trainers and coaches who see the athlete daily and a written trigger for what happens when they flag him.

## Do not apply when

- The data are pitchers (baseball overhead throwing); do not transfer elbow torque, UCL return rates or pitch-count figures to football or other sports.
- The youth findings (500 pitchers, over 100 innings) are not college-level thresholds; do not set a college innings limit from them.
- The 4 to 1, 5 to 1 and 36 to 1 odds are retrospective and recall-based; do not treat them as causal or as predictive risk scores for an individual.
- Reference ranges defined by high velocity and health are partly circular, and the talk reports poor mechanics predicted injury about half the time [58:38]; do not use an out-of-range value to restrict an athlete by itself.
- Sample sizes are small and partly unpublished (38 pitchers in one study, the spring training work); do not generalize a result from one or two studies.
- Vendor devices shown (motion tools from a company the speaker advises) were not validated in the talk [41:13].

## First step

List the last two seasons' return-to-performance cases and write, for each, the four pieces from the talk (did they return, did they stay healthy, stats versus age-matched expectation, time to return) in a simple sheet. Do not share it until you have checked it against Athletic Medicine records.
